To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
astrocytes in the human postnatal brain develop from an immature to a mature form and that the glial vascular and the glial limiting membranes have a supporting function.

the postnatal maturation of the fibrillary astrocye is characterized by the development of the dense fibrocytic network and that this process takes place during the postnatal myelinization of the white matter.
the GFAP immunoperoxidose staining of the postnatal brain shows that the astrocytes in the white matter of the central nervous system are the main supporting cells of the myelinated fibers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and function of the astrocyte in the postnatal human brain.
the normal postnatal development of astrocytes.
the development of the glial limiting membranes and the glial fibrous network.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the astrocytes in the central nervous system of children without anamnestic signs of disease are in a normal state of development.
the postnatal development of astrocytes is completed during the first 14 years of life.

the GFAP-immunoreactive astrocytic network is the main structural element of the central nervous system and is involved in a variety of functions, including the maintenance of the blood-brain barrier, the guidance of neuronal migration and the support of the myelinating oligodendrocytes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the postnatal astrocytic development in the central nervous system is a dynamic process.
the astrocytic fibrillar network of the central nervous system is a dynamic system which changes during the life span and which is capable to adapt to various circumstances.
the astrocytes have a very important supporting function during the development of the central nervous system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
astrocytes play an important role in brain development and function.
the astrocytes of children with no anamnestic disease or signs of disease at autopsy are very similar to those in adults, but the glial network is less dense.
astrocytes are a dynamic population of cells in the CNS that can respond to injury or insult by changing their morphology, gene expression, and function.
